subject: Child Development & Pedagogy
stem: A child avoids eye contact, shows repetitive hand movements, and becomes distressed by unexpected changes in the daily routine. These signs are most characteristic of:

options.option_text: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)
Intellectual disability alone
Hearing impairment
Visual impairment

explanation: Difficulty with eye contact/social interaction, repetitive behaviours (stimming), and resistance to change in routine are core, well-documented ASD indicators — distinct from intellectual disability, which centres on general cognitive/adaptive functioning delays.

subject: Child Development & Pedagogy
stem: For a child with hearing impairment included in a regular classroom, which teaching strategy is most appropriate?

options.option_text: Facing the child while speaking, using visual aids and possibly sign language/lip-reading support
Always speaking with your back turned to the class while writing on the board
Relying exclusively on audio recordings with no visual support
Excluding the child from all classroom discussions

explanation: Facing the child (enabling lip-reading), using visual cues, and reasonable accommodations (like sign-language interpretation where available) support genuine access to instruction — turning away or excluding the child removes access entirely.

subject: Child Development & Pedagogy
stem: For a child with visual impairment, which resource is a standard tool used to enable independent reading and writing of text?

options.option_text: Braille script and Braille slate/writing tools
Sign language exclusively
Lip-reading training
Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS) only

explanation: Braille is the standard tactile reading/writing system for children with visual impairment. Sign language and lip-reading serve hearing-impaired learners; PECS is commonly used to support communication in some children with autism/limited speech.

subject: Child Development & Pedagogy
stem: For a child with intellectual disability, the most effective instructional approach generally involves:

options.option_text: Breaking tasks into small, sequential steps with concrete materials and repeated practice
Presenting all content abstractly with no concrete support
Expecting the same pace of learning as same-age peers with no adaptation
Removing all structure and routine from lessons

explanation: Task analysis (breaking complex skills into small steps), concrete/hands-on materials, and repeated guided practice are core strategies for intellectual disability — the opposite of abstract-only, unmodified-pace instruction.

subject: Child Development & Pedagogy
stem: An Individualised Education Plan (IEP) for a child with a disability is best described as:

options.option_text: A customised plan of goals, accommodations and teaching strategies tailored to that specific child's needs
The exact same lesson plan used for the entire class without any change
A punishment record for a child's misbehaviour
A document used only once and never reviewed again

explanation: An IEP is individualised — set collaboratively (teacher, specialists, parents) with specific goals and accommodations for that child, and reviewed/updated periodically — not a generic class-wide document or a disciplinary record.

subject: Child Development & Pedagogy
stem: Specific Learning Disabilities such as dyslexia, dysgraphia and dyscalculia are officially recognised as disabilities under which Indian legislation (2016)?

options.option_text: Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016
Right to Education Act, 2009
Right to Information Act, 2005
Juvenile Justice Act, 2015

explanation: The RPwD Act, 2016 explicitly lists Specific Learning Disabilities (including dyslexia, dysgraphia, dyscalculia) among its 21 recognised disability categories, entitling affected children to accommodations and benefits.
